## Overview

The Hadiya are an ethnic group native to Ethiopia’s southern region who speak Hadiyya. The 2007 Ethiopian national census reported that 1,269,382 people identified themselves as Hadiya, including 150,087 urban inhabitants; 93.9% lived in the Southern Nations, Nationalities, and People’s Region. Hadiya-inhabited areas extend from the upper Gibe in the west to the bend of the Wabi Šäbälle in the east, across the western edge of the Ethiopian Rift Valley and adjoining highlands. Historically, many groups belonged to the Hadiya Sultanate, but after its break-up they became separate ethnic groups with different languages and cultural affiliations. Hadiya culture is documented here especially through language, traditional songs, historical political institutions, and religious change.

## Music & performance

Hadiyya has a documented tradition of traditional songs. In their English-language book published in 1999, Braukämper and Mishago compiled a collection of what the source describes as the presently vanishing art of traditional songs of Hadiyya. The lyrics follow a strict rule of Hadiyya traditional poetry in which rhythmical rhyming occurs at the beginning of the verse.

## Festivals & rituals

Hadiya people were mainly Muslim or practiced indigenous beliefs known as *Fandaanano* in the 13th–16th centuries. The sources state that the conquest of Menelik II in the 19th century contributed to conversions to Orthodox Christianity, while Protestant (*P'ent'ay*) missionaries increased in the late 1930s. The sources also describe historical religious conflict and political change, including the participation of Hadiya rulers and troops in the sixteenth-century invasion of Ethiopia associated with Adal.

## Oral tradition & literature

Hadiyya was historically an oral language. The language source identifies a collection of traditional songs and describes their poetic structure, including rhythmical rhyming at the beginning of the verse. The Hadiya language article also states that Hadiyya is now written using a Latin-based orthography developed for educational and administrative use.

Historical knowledge appears in written and oral forms. Hadiya elders describe a dynasty founded by descendants of Harar Emir Abadir who intermarried with Sidama. The earliest surviving mention of Hadiya is in the *Kebra Nagast*, chapter 94, while another early account appears in a manuscript written on the island monastery of Lake Hayq. Hadiya history is also recorded in chronicles, including accounts of Amano, Garad Mahiko, Eleni of Hadiya, and the Hadiya Sultanate.

## Language & religion

Hadiyya, called Hadiyyisa by its speakers, is a Highland East Cushitic language of the Afroasiatic family. It is also known in the sources as Hadiyigna, Adiya, Adea, Adiye, Hadia, Hadiya, and Hadya. Over 1.2 million people speak it, and most speakers live in the Hadiya Zone of the Southern Nations, Nationalities, and People’s Region. The language has four recognized dialects: Leemo, Badawacho, Shashogo, and Sooro. These dialects are mutually intelligible with slight regional variations.

Hadiyya was historically oral and is now written with a Latin-based orthography. It was formerly written using the traditional Ethiopic syllabary. The New Testament of the Christian Bible was translated into Hadiyya and published by the Bible Society of Ethiopia in 1993.

Historically, Hadiya people practiced Islam and indigenous beliefs known as *Fandaanano*. Later religious landscapes included Orthodox Christianity and Protestant Christianity.
